newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: LME copper/aluminium extend gains in Asian trade.
newsitem.headline: LME copper/aluminium extend gains in Asian trade.

text.p: Three-month London Metal Exchange (LME) copper prices extended their recent gains in Asian trade on Wednesday following a strong technical close in London, Far East traders said on Wednesday.
Three-month copper rose $5 a tonne to $2,535/$2,540 at 0215 GMT in early Asian trade from $2,530/$2,535 at Tuesday's late LME close.
LME broker Brandeis said in its daily report that the 10-day moving average should now provide good support for copper as prices look to challenge the recent high of $2,548 a tonne.
A trader in Seoul pegged support for three-month copper at $2,461.
"We think copper has already completed its short term orrection and expect it to start again on a bullish trend with help from favourable technicals," a trader with a local brokerage firm said.

Brandeis said aluminium prices are also likely to rise further on continuing LME stocks fall and data from the IPAI, which showed that total stocks of all forms of aluminium fell by 49,000 tonnes to 3.047 million tonnes at the end of April.
This compared with 3.096 million tonnes in March this year and 3.514 million tonnes in April 1996.
Three-month aluminium bid prices rose $2 a tonne to $1,623 at 0300 GMT in Asian trade from $1,621 at Wednesday's late LME close.
Brandeis said the next target on the upside for aluminium was pegged around $1,620 and then at the 30-day moving average at $1,614. Support was still seen at $1,600 and then $1,580.

Another LME broker, Macquarie said gains in aluminium prices have not fully reflected LME stock draw-downs for several reasons, including concerns about possible restarts of idle production capacity estimated to total 800,000 tonnes a year.

Macquarie said other reasons included producers forward selling into any rally above $1,650 basis three-months, worries about weaker demand in the second half of the year and concerns about the build-up of large "hidden" stocks by banks and traders.
